items.title: Chuck Israels interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2021
items.q: I find Bobby Brookmeyer a kind of a difficult person because he’s full of dichotomies.

ctx.x: It’s a challenge you know, because we say okay we have an intro, then we do the head, whatever it is, and we’ll do the bridge. And if you’re A-A-B-A, and then you get to that spot, now I have a shout chorus in mind, but I can’t do it yet.

Yeah maybe, yeah. I also, I understand his position about that. I find Bobby Brookmeyer a kind of a difficult person because he’s full of dichotomies. He has done extraordinarily beautiful work and some obtuse stuff that I just don’t understand at all. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

items.title: Chuck Israels interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2021
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] I’m reminded of a quote, Dave Rivello, who is at Eastman School of Music, attributed to Bob Brookmeyer. And he said, “When you write a big band arrangement try to put off as long as can the solo.” [INTERVIEWEE] Oh well, it depends. I mean I guess, maybe.

ctx.x: You shut up and live with it usually. It depends on the circumstance. There are circumstances in which you can stop and fix it. Most people don’t do that intentionally but it has happened. It happened at a concert with the National Jazz Ensemble I think in Buffalo, I think it was a concert and Gunther Schuller was there and after the concert I talked to him about it and we both had the same response, and it was a couple of alto saxophone players got into a saxophone battle that might have been — the idea of a…

I’m reminded of a quote, Dave Rivello, who is at Eastman School of Music, attributed to Bob Brookmeyer. And he said, “When you write a big band arrangement try to put off as long as you can the solo.”
Oh well, it depends. I mean I guess, maybe.
